In that case, the differences in processing time between pro and anti trials were 24 ms for the aggregate curves from Experiments 1 and 2, and 34 ms for the aggregate curves from Experiments 3 and 4.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by alternative analysis of the experimental data.

claims.claim: The informed antisaccades were consistently delayed even in Experiment 4, in which motor plans were strongly biased toward the non-cue by the early exogenous signal.
claims.source: Most notably, the informed antisaccades were consistently delayed even in Experiment 4, in which motor plans were strongly biased toward the non-cue by the early exogenous signal (Figure 3c, Figure 2—figure supplement 3d).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claims.claim: Producing an informed antisaccade required about 30 ms more of processing time than producing a similarly informed prosaccade, but this number varied by an additional amount in proportion to the strength of the initial bias toward or away from the cue.
claims.source: So, in general, producing an informed antisaccade required about 30 ms more of processing time than producing a similarly informed prosaccade, but this number varied by an additional amount in proportion to the strength of the initial bias toward or away from the cue.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the relationship between processing-time cost and motor bias.

claims.claim: In Experiment 4, pro trials demonstrate significantly higher accuracy than anti trials in the transition range in spite of the fact that, during the preceding capture interval, pro trials were at a huge disadvantage.
claims.source: Again, the most notable result is for Experiment 4: in that case, pro trials demonstrate significantly higher accuracy than anti trials in the transition range (Figure 7e, orange points) in spite of the fact that, during the preceding capture interval, pro trials were at a huge disadvantage (Figure 7d; compare blue vs. red bars in C and T ranges).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7d and 7e.

claims.claim: The main consequence of the motor bias was to induce an asymmetry in timing and accuracy between pro- and antisaccades.
claims.source: Thus, the bias did not incur an obvious disadvantage in terms of average success in the task. Its main consequence was simply to induce an asymmetry in timing and accuracy between pro- and antisaccades (Figures 6c and 7f).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of the relationship between motor bias and performance.

results.result: The manuscript reviews established knowledge about the bidirectional coupling between saccades and visuospatial attention, noting that while saccade planning commits attention to the endpoint (presaccadic attention), the reverse relationship—how endogenous attention influences saccade planning—is less clear and can be dissociated.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C9 accurately summarize well-established findings from the literature with appropriate citations. These claims provide necessary background context and are supported by extensive prior research, though they represent prior work rather than novel findings from this study.

results.result: Prior work by the authors demonstrated that exogenous and endogenous signals in urgent pro/antisaccade tasks act at different times and independently, with exogenous responses manifesting as early involuntary captured saccades (~100 ms) and endogenous responses as later deliberate rises in performance (~150 ms).
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C12 accurately describe findings from the authors' earlier publications (cited as Salinas et al., 2019; Goldstein et al., 2022). These claims establish the foundation for the current study and are appropriately attributed to prior work.

results.result: Exogenous capture was successfully manipulated by varying cue and non-cue luminances: equal luminances minimized capture (performance near chance at ~100 ms rPT), while luminance differences reinstated capture as transient biases toward the brighter stimulus, peaking at ~100 ms and dissipating by ~150 ms, demonstrating independence of exogenous and endogenous influences.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C18 are well-supported by the tachometric curves in Figure 2 showing clear luminance-dependent effects. The experimental manipulation successfully isolated exogenous from endogenous components, with appropriate statistical support (n=11 reliable performers) and consistent patterns across conditions.

results.result: Individual variability in exogenous capture ranged from 0-100%, but the magnitude was symmetric between pro and anti trials (p=0.8 across participants, p=0.5 and p=0.2 for pooled trials), confirming that exogenous signals track luminance regardless of task rules, with effects occurring in an 83-124 ms window.
results.evaluation: Claims C19, C21, and C51 are supported by Figure 3 data with appropriate statistical tests. The symmetry analysis provides strong evidence that exogenous capture is stimulus-driven rather than task-dependent. However, the choice of the 83-124 ms window, while data-driven, involves some circularity as it was defined based on the same data being analyzed.

results.result: Antisaccades consistently required 25-35 ms more processing time than prosaccades to reach comparable performance criteria, with rise points of 165 ms (pro) vs 194 ms (anti) for Experiments 1+2 and 152 ms (pro) vs 187 ms (anti) for Experiments 3+4, even when exogenous signals biased against the antisaccade.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C56 are well-supported by multiple converging analyses (Figure 4) including individual rise points (p=0.008, n=11), aggregate curves with bootstrapped confidence intervals, and alternative criterion-based measures (24-34 ms differences). The consistency across different analytical approaches and experimental conditions strengthens the conclusion. The n=11 sample after applying modulation criteria is adequate but represents a subset of participants.

results.result: Fifteen of 18 participants showed a motor bias toward the attended cue location during early guesses (rPT ≤75 ms), with the mean fraction of cue-directed guesses significantly above 0.5 across participants (p=0.00006), experimental conditions (p=0.00003), and pooled trials (p=10^-48).
results.evaluation: Claim C26 is strongly supported by Figure 5 data with robust statistical evidence across multiple levels of analysis. The effect is highly significant and consistent, though individual variability is substantial (3 of 18 participants showed opposite bias).

results.result: The processing-time cost for antisaccades (~30 ms baseline) varied proportionally with initial motor bias strength (correlation ρ=0.59, p=0.026), with an expected 27 ms cost at zero bias, though the bias primarily induced timing/accuracy asymmetries rather than overall performance deficits.
results.evaluation: Claims C29, C57, and C59 are supported by regression analysis in Figure 6c showing moderate positive correlation. The 27 ms intercept provides evidence for a baseline cost independent of bias. However, the correlation is moderate (ρ=0.59) with n=12 participants meeting fit criteria, and the relationship could be influenced by individual differences in task strategy.

results.result: During the transition range (135-200 ms rPT), prosaccades showed consistently higher accuracy than antisaccades across all experiments (p<10^-5 pooled, p≤0.003 individual experiments), including Experiment 4 where exogenous capture strongly disadvantaged prosaccades.
results.evaluation: Claims C30 and C58 are well-supported by Figure 7e data with strong statistical evidence. The finding in Experiment 4 is particularly compelling as it demonstrates the endogenous effect persists even when opposing a strong exogenous bias, though the transition range definition (135-200 ms) is somewhat arbitrary.

results.result: The study concludes that generating correct antisaccades requires ~30 ms more processing time than prosaccades, and that saccade plans during fixation are biased toward endogenously attended locations but with weak coupling that can be rapidly overridden.
results.evaluation: Claims C34 and C35 represent the main conclusions, well-supported by converging evidence from multiple analyses (Figures 4-7). The ~30 ms estimate is consistent across different analytical approaches. The characterization of 'weak' coupling is justified by the rapid override capability and individual variability, though 'weak' is somewhat subjective.

results.result: The observed weak coupling between endogenous attention and saccade planning is consistent with prior dissociation studies, and the 20-40 ms time costs are remarkably similar to those reported by Belopolsky and Theeuwes (2009) despite very different reaction time ranges.
results.evaluation: Claims C36 and C37 appropriately contextualize the findings within existing literature. The comparison to Belopolsky and Theeuwes (2009) is valid and strengthens the interpretation, though the tasks differ substantially in design and the convergence could be coincidental.

results.result: In Experiments 3 and 4, tachometric curves showed a 'downward rebound' after exogenous capture, suggesting that if an exogenous signal doesn't trigger a saccade within tens of milliseconds, the corresponding motor plan is rapidly suppressed, potentially reflecting a general mechanism where attention shifts activate motor plans that are either executed or quickly suppressed.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C40 describe an interesting pattern in the data (visible in Figure 2c,d and supplements), but C39 and C40 are speculative interpretations ('as if', 'perhaps', 'it appears'). The downward rebound is real but the mechanistic explanation is not directly tested. Alternative explanations (e.g., statistical artifacts, task-specific strategies) are not ruled out.

results.result: The authors argue that behavior in prosaccade/antisaccade tasks is fundamentally determined by the magnitudes and spatial/temporal alignment of exogenous and endogenous signals rather than specific task instructions, supported by prior work showing that prefrontal cortex responses during antisaccades can be predicted from simpler tasks.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C44 present a theoretical framework supported by appropriate citations. C42 is an inference/interpretation rather than a direct finding, but it's reasonable given the data. C43 and C44 appropriately cite Zhu et al. (2024) to support the generalizability of the framework, though this relies on cross-species extrapolation (monkey to human).

results.result: The urgent task design with processing time (rPT) analysis reveals that attentional dynamics evolve much more rapidly than typically appreciated, with saccades shifting direction within 30-50 ms, recapitulating phenomena from prior studies (transient salience effects, stimulus/goal-driven dissociation) but on faster timescales.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C48 are supported by the tachometric curve data showing rapid transitions. C46 appropriately cites prior work, and C47-C48 are justified conclusions from the observed dynamics. The urgent paradigm does provide superior temporal resolution compared to traditional RT-based approaches, though the claim that dynamics are 'more rapid than generally appreciated' is somewhat subjective.

results.result: Eighteen participants (11 female, 7 male, median age 28, range 24-63) completed all four experiments, generating eight experimental conditions per participant.
results.evaluation: Claim C49 is a straightforward methodological description that is adequately documented. Sample size is reasonable for this type of psychophysical study, though the age range is quite broad which could introduce variability.

results.result: The study demonstrates temporal dissociation between exogenous and endogenous attention signals in urgent saccade tasks. Exogenous capture occurs early (~100 ms), is luminance-dependent, and involuntary, while endogenous responses emerge later (~150 ms) and align with task goals. These signals act independently across processing time.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm this core finding. Reviewer 1 states the authors 'capitalize on their novel urgent saccade task to dissociate the effects of endogenous and exogenous attention' and notes 'the behavioral interplay of two forms of attention...are illustrated at the level of tens of milliseconds.' Reviewer 2 confirms 'the findings...indicate that saccade planning is influenced by the locus of endogenous attention, but that this influence was short-lasting.' The editor describes the evidence as 'convincing.'

results.result: Individual variability in exogenous capture ranged dramatically from 0% to 100% across participants, but the exogenous signal consistently tracked the higher luminance stimulus regardless of task rule (pro vs. anti).
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these findings about individual differences or the luminance-tracking property of exogenous signals. Reviewer 1 emphasizes the study's strength in 'carefully measure[ing] the time course' across 'well-controlled experimental conditions,' implicitly accepting the reported variability and consistency patterns.

results.result: Antisaccades consistently required 25-35 ms more processing time than prosaccades to reach comparable performance criteria, indicating obligatory coupling between saccade plans and endogenous attention. This delay persisted even when motor plans were strongly biased by exogenous signals.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'the findings...indicate that saccade planning is influenced by the locus of endogenous attention,' directly supporting the coupling claim. Reviewer 1 notes the authors 'make meaningful claims about the time course of visual behavior, attention, and the potential neural mechanisms at a timescale relevant to everyday human behavior,' affirming the temporal precision of these measurements. No reviewer challenges the 25-35 ms estimate.

results.result: Most participants (15/18) showed a motor bias toward the cue location during fixation. This bias correlated with processing-time costs: stronger bias toward the cue increased the cost for antisaccades but decreased it for prosaccades. The expected cost at zero bias was 27 ms.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings without challenge. Reviewer 1 emphasizes the study's ability to 'carefully measure the time course of the interaction between attention and eye movements in various well-controlled experimental conditions,' which encompasses these bias-related measurements. The editor describes the evidence as 'convincing.'

results.result: During the transition period between exogenous and endogenous control, prosaccades showed consistently higher accuracy than antisaccades across experiments, even when prosaccades were at a disadvantage during the preceding capture interval.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question this finding. Reviewer 1 notes the study 'illustrate[s]' attention dynamics 'at the level of tens of milliseconds as they interact with the planning and execution of saccades,' implicitly accepting the detailed temporal patterns including transition-period differences.

results.result: Generating a correct antisaccade requires ~30 ms more processing time than a prosaccade. Saccade plans during fixation are biased toward endogenously attended locations, but this coupling is weak and can be rapidly overridden, consistent with prior dissociation studies.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 directly confirms 'saccade planning is influenced by the locus of endogenous attention, but that this influence was short-lasting and could be overcome quickly,' precisely matching the authors' conclusion. Reviewer 1 affirms the authors 'find that attention and eye movements are, to some extent, linked to one another but that this link is transient.' No concerns are raised about the ~30 ms estimate or the weak coupling interpretation.

results.result: When saccades are strongly biased, tachometric curves show a brief reversal after exogenous capture, suggesting that shifts of spatial attention (both exogenous and endogenous) activate motor plans that are either executed within tens of milliseconds or rapidly suppressed.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this observation or interpretation. Reviewer 1 notes the study reveals 'the behavioral interplay of two forms of attention...at the level of tens of milliseconds,' which encompasses these rapid reversal dynamics. The speculative mechanism is presented as interpretation rather than definitive claim, and reviewers accept it within that framing.

results.result: The urgent saccade paradigm with early gap removal and processing time analysis reveals that spatial attention dynamics in oculomotor circuits vary more rapidly than generally appreciated, with saccade direction reversing within 30-50 ms as distinct mechanisms interact.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly states the study's findings 'reveal new dynamics between endogenous attention and eye movement control and lead the way for studying them using experiments under time-pressure,' directly endorsing the methodological and conceptual advance. Reviewer 1 emphasizes the study's strength in measuring 'the time course...at a timescale relevant to everyday human behavior.' The editor calls the study 'important' and the evidence 'convincing.'

results.result: The fundamental factors determining behavior in prosaccade/antisaccade tasks are the magnitudes and spatial/temporal alignment of exogenous and endogenous signals. At the circuit level, target selection dynamics are dictated by the relative strengths and congruency of these activations.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this integrative framework. Reviewer 1 states the results 'allow the authors to make meaningful claims about...the potential neural mechanisms,' affirming the circuit-level interpretation. Reviewer 2 notes the study advances understanding of 'their control by brain mechanisms for attention.' The editor describes the study as advancing understanding of 'cortical mechanisms of eye movements and the cognitive process of attention.'

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C30 and C58 regarding endogenous effects persisting in transition periods. Both evaluations find the evidence convincing and well-supported, with peer reviewers accepting the temporal precision of these measurements.

Both address claims C38-C40 about rapid reversal dynamics. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to speculative interpretations and lack of alternative explanations, while peer reviewers SUPPORT the claims, accepting them as reasonable interpretations within the study's framing.

Perfect agreement on claims C45-C48 regarding methodological advances and rapid dynamics. Both evaluations strongly support the urgent paradigm's contribution to revealing faster-than-appreciated attention-saccade dynamics, with peer reviewers explicitly endorsing the methodological innovation.

Strong agreement on claims C23, C25, C53-C56 regarding the ~25-35 ms coupling estimate. Both evaluations find converging evidence convincing. OpenEval notes the reduced sample size (n=11) as a minor limitation, while peer reviewers emphasize the temporal precision without raising concerns about sample size.

Both address claims C29, C57, C59 regarding bias-cost relationships. OpenEval supports findings but notes moderate correlation strength and potential individual differences. Peer reviewers accept these findings without challenge, emphasizing the careful measurement of temporal interactions.

Strong agreement on claims C42-C44 regarding theoretical framework and neural mechanisms. Both evaluations support the integrative circuit-level interpretation, with peer reviewers explicitly affirming the meaningful claims about potential neural mechanisms.

Both address claims C13-C18 about luminance-dependent effects and exogenous-endogenous dissociation. OpenEval supports with detailed statistical validation. Peer result R1 also covers C10-C12 (prior work foundation), affirming the overall experimental approach and temporal precision.

Both address claims C19 and C21 regarding individual differences and stimulus-driven exogenous capture. OpenEval notes minor circularity in window selection but supports findings. Peer reviewers accept these patterns without challenge, implicitly endorsing the reported variability.

Both address main conclusions C34-C35 about weak coupling and ~30 ms estimate. Complete agreement that evidence is convincing and well-supported by converging analyses. Peer reviewers directly confirm the transient nature of the attention-saccade link.

Both address claims C36-C37 contextualizing findings within existing literature. OpenEval supports the comparison to Belopolsky & Theeuwes (2009) while noting task differences. Peer result R6 focuses more on C34-C35 but implicitly accepts the broader contextualization.

OpenEval R2 addresses claims C10-C12 about prior work foundation, rating as SUPPORTED. Peer result R1 covers these same claims plus C13-C18, affirming the novel urgent saccade task builds appropriately on earlier publications.

Both address claim C26 regarding endogenous bias effects. OpenEval provides detailed statistical validation while noting individual variability. Peer result R4 also covers C29, C57, C59 and accepts all bias-related findings as part of carefully measured temporal interactions.

OpenEval R1 addresses claims C1-C9 about well-established background literature. These represent prior work context rather than novel findings. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these background claims.

OpenEval R14 addresses claim C49 about methodological details (sample size, age range). This straightforward methodological description is supported but not specifically evaluated in peer review results.
